paper.citation: Southey B, Willshire M, Connick MJ, Austin D, Spits D, Beckman E. Reactive Strength Index as a Key Performance Indicator in Different Athlete Populations - A Systematic Review. Science & Sports. 2023.
paper.abstract: A systematic review of 19 studies (872 participants, mean ages 17 to 27 years) comparing drop-jump reactive strength index (RSI) between athlete populations. Moderate to large differences were found between populations, with the strength of differences varying by comparison.
paper.tldr: RSI differs between athlete populations, with sprint and power athletes, males, high achievers and elite athletes generally scoring higher, and relative strength appears to be an influencing factor.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with five databases searched on 25 August 2021 and 865 records screened to 19 included studies. Studies were eligible only if they used a bilateral drop jump and made cross-sectional cohort comparisons, and injury comparisons and intervention studies were excluded. Quality was rated on a modified 10-item Downs and Black checklist (scores 6 to 9, median 8); no meta-analysis was performed.
paper.findings: Males had moderately greater RSI than females (effect size 0.7 to 1.04, two studies). Sprint and power athletes had higher RSI than athletes in tennis, soccer, endurance running, hockey and rugby (effect sizes 0.73 to 3.98). Forwards and backs comparisons showed moderate differences (effect sizes 0.84 to 1.17), with heavier positions tending to have lower RSI. Seven studies found large to very large RSI differences between high and low achievers or elite and sub-elite athletes.
paper.limitations: This is a qualitative synthesis without pooled effect sizes, and cohort comparisons cannot establish causation. Drop heights (20 to 60 cm) and RSI calculations varied, so values could not be standardised. External validity could be confirmed in only one of 19 studies, only 5 of 19 reported strength training history, and five studies did not report participant sex.
paper.practicalImplications: RSI can be used as a population-referenced comparison, but between-group differences should not be read as predictors of an individual's performance. The authors suggest that developing relative strength may be a route to improving reactive strength, though they could not determine cause and effect. Staff should use RSI norms cautiously because drop heights and calculations differ across studies.
paper.athleteDev: Relative strength appears to be linked to higher RSI across populations, so programs aiming to raise reactive strength may include relative strength work, although causation is not confirmed. Comparisons with RSI norms should account for differences in drop height and calculation method.
paper.rtp: The review excluded studies comparing injured athletes and did not assess return to sport, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or to interpret RSI after injury.
